text:
1. PRIMARY DIAGNOSIS
- Root cause: Intermittent thermal overload of the CNC motion controller or stepper/servo driver caused by a degraded cooling fan and clogged heatsink/filter, with high humidity accelerating moisture-related leakage or signal noise. Confidence: 85%.
- No diagnostic trouble codes were captured or stored; this diagnosis leans entirely on the observed symptom pattern (mid-job stalls with no alarm, recovery after reboot) and environmental clues (noisy fan, high humidity). Thermal failures in microcontroller-based circuits often do not set a fault code because the processor resets before logging a fault, or the power interruption is too brief to trigger a watchdog alarm.
- Failure physics: The controller fan bearing develops wear over thousands of hours, producing audible noise and reducing RPM. Airflow drops below the minimum required to keep heatsinks and ICs within safe temperatures (typically below 65–70°C junction). As the node finishes a heavy machining pass, internal temperature crosses the thermal trip point of the CPU, motion ASIC, or voltage regulator, causing a momentary lockup or reset. The machine stops as if paused, but no active alarm is generated because the logic circuit resets and resumes before the safety relay times out. High humidity compounds this by promoting moisture absorption into dust bridges on the PCB; at 70%+ RH, surface leakage currents can corrupt high-impedance digital signals (step/direction, encoder feedback), producing spurious missed steps or a hung state that clears on reboot. The noisy fan is the strongest physical clue: increased bearing friction is the most common precursor to complete fan failure.
- Age/hours: Unknown, but fan bearings in industrial enclosures typically fail between 20,000 and 50,000 operating hours. If the machine has run daily for 2–3 years, fan degradation is expected.

2. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS
- Alternative cause 1 (likely): Power supply ripple/sag under load — the DC supply capacitors aging cause voltage dips on the 5V or 24V logic rail during axis movement, triggering a controller brown-out. Rules in: if a DMM on min/max mode catches a drop >5% during jogging. Rules out: if the stall occurs even when no axis is moving (e.g., during spindle-only cutting). This can set identical symptoms; shops often misdiagnose it as a bad controller board.
- Alternative cause 2 (moderately likely): Ground-loop or EMI noise — high humidity lowers insulation resistance, allowing spindle VFD noise to couple onto controller signal lines, causing intermittent hung states. Rules in: stall occurs only when spindle is running at certain RPMs; an oscilloscope shows >200 mV noise spikes on the step line. Rules out: stall happens even with spindle off during dry runs.
- Alternative cause 3 (less likely): Loose internal connector or cold solder joint — vibration and thermal cycling create an intermittent open on a motion-control cable. Rules in: stall can be triggered by gently wiggling the controller wiring harness; resistance measurement across connector pins fluctuates. Rules out: stall is perfectly correlated with “controller run time since power-up,” pointing to thermal, not mechanical.
- Alternative cause 4 (low): Faulty motor driver overheating and entering thermal foldback — the driver itself shuts down, causing axis stall but the controller may not flag an alarm if the fault signal isn’t wired. Rules in: the driver’s fault LED blinks or the driver case temperature exceeds 70°C. Rules out: swapping the driver with a known-good unit eliminates stalls.
- Equipment-specific pattern: On custom CNC routers using generic stepper drivers and a Windows/PC-based controller, the most common “stall no alarm” root cause is PC/controller overheating, often initiated by a failing chassis fan or dust-filled CPU heatsink.

3. DIAGNOSTIC VERIFICATION
- Do these tests in order; each is non-invasive. A fair labor budget for complete verification is 1.0–1.5 hours at the regional industrial control rate of $100–$150/hour (total diagnostic cost $100–$225).
- Test 1: Visual & thermal inspection of controller enclosure. Tool: Infrared thermometer or thermal camera plus a flashlight. Remove the cabinet side panel, check for dust, clogged filter, and fan rotation when powered. Measure the temperature of the largest heatsink and the ambient air intake. Pass: intake-to-heatsink delta <15°C, and heatsink temp <60°C after 20 min of a typical program. Fail: delta >20°C or heatsink >65°C.
- Test 2: Fan RPM/airflow verification. Tool: optical tachometer or anemometer. Measure fan speed and compare to the rating on the fan label (usually 3000–5000 RPM for 80 mm fans). Pass: within 15% of rated RPM, and airflow feels brisk. Fail: RPM below 70% of rated, or bearing grinds when spun by hand.
- Test 3: DC supply rail voltage under load. Tool: Digital multimeter with Min/Max capture or an oscilloscope. Monitor the 24V, 12V, and 5V lines at the controller’s power connector while jogging all axes simultaneously. Pass: voltage sag less than 5% and AC ripple <100 mV peak-to-peak on 5V. Fail: any drop >0.3V on 5V or ripple >150 mV.
- Test 4: Environmental stress test. Run the machine with the controller cabinet open and an external box fan blowing directly on the electronics. If stalls stop or reduce drastically, thermal cause is confirmed. This is the ONE test that must be completed and shown to the customer before any part is purchased; it isolates the root cause with zero cost.
- Test cost: Test 1–3 combined take about 0.5 hr; test 4 adds 0.3 hr. Total diagnostic time 0.8 hr, typical cost $80–$120. If a shop quotes more than 1.5 hr for these non-invasive checks, ask for a breakdown.

4. SHOP INTERROGATION
- Question 1: “Can you show me the temperature readings inside the controller cabinet when the stall happened? What was the heatsink temperature vs. ambient?”
  - Competent answer: “We logged it with a thermocouple/data logger; here is the graph showing it hit 68°C right before the fault.”
  - Red-flag: “We didn’t measure that, but it’s just a bad board.”
- Question 2: “What is the DC ripple on the 5V logic rail measured with an oscilloscope under full axis load?”
  - Competent answer: “We captured 60 mV peak-to-peak; well within the 100 mV limit.”
  - Red-flag: “We don’t have a scope; we just checked voltage with a meter.”
- Question 3: “Did you verify the airflow of the fan with a tachometer or anemometer? What RPM did you measure?”
  - Competent answer: “The fan label says 4000 RPM; ours measured 2200 RPM — clearly failing.”
  - Red-flag: “The fan spins, so it’s fine.”
- Question 4: “Can I see the freeze-frame or event log from the motion controller showing the state of the machine at the instant it stalled?”
  - Competent answer: “Here is the log — servo enabled, no fault bit set, position frozen — consistent with a controller lock-up.”
  - Red-flag: “That controller doesn’t have logs, we just know it’s bad.”
- Question 5: “Please show me the voltage drop test on the power and ground wiring from the supply to the controller during a heavy cut.”
  - Competent answer: “Drop was 0.15V on the 24V line; below 0.25V max.”
  - Red-flag: “We didn’t do that.”
- Artifacts they must physically show: infrared thermal image of the PCB, oscilloscope screenshot of the 5V rail, measured fan RPM reading, and the old fan (if replaced).

5. CONVERSATION SCRIPTING
- Opening: “I’ve been dealing with these random stalls, and I noticed the fan is getting loud. I’d like to start by checking if heat is the simple root cause before we go into expensive parts. Can we do that?”
- Phrasing (curiosity): “I’m curious — with the high humidity and that noisy fan, could the controller be overheating just enough to hiccup without throwing a fault? Have you seen that on other routers?”
- Example dialogue for highest-value question: “Could you show me the temperature of the controller’s heatsink during a normal run and right before a stall? I’ve read that when these CPU-based controllers get past 65°C, they can glitch without an alarm. I’d feel a lot better if we ruled that out first.”
- Handling defensiveness: “I get that without a fault code it’s tricky. I’m not saying you’re wrong — I just want to see the thermal and voltage data so I’m comfortable. I’d rather pay for an hour of diagnostic time that points to the exact part than guess at a $2,000 board.”
- Exit strategy: “Thanks for checking. I’m going to think about it and maybe have another tech run a few simple tests. I’ll be in touch.”
- NEVER say: “My AI report says…” or “I got a second opinion online.” ALWAYS say: “I’ve done some research and just want to understand the measurements.”

6. COST BREAKDOWN
- Itemized parts: Replacement cooling fan — quality aftermarket (e.g., Sunon, Delta, NMB, 24VDC, matching size: commonly 80×80×25 mm or 40×40×10 mm) $15–$40 based on DigiKey/Mouser pricing. If the controller manufacturer supplies an OEM-branded fan with proprietary connector, it could be $50–$120 from the CNC supplier. No part number available without knowing the controller brand; a generic 80 mm 24V 0.15A fan can be sourced for $20.
- Labor: Replacing the fan, cleaning filters, blowing out heatsinks, and verifying operation — estimated job time 0.5–1.0 hour. This is based on typical hands-on time for an electronics tech, not a formal book time (no standard for custom CNC). At $100–$150/hour, labor is $50–$150.
- Diagnostic fee: 0.5–1.0 hour should be charged, but standard practice in industrial repair is to credit the diagnostic fee toward repair if you approve the work. Ask beforehand.
- Fair total price range: $80–$220 (fan $20 + 1 hr labor $150 max, including a 0.5 hr diagnostic that’s credited). If a filter kit is needed, add $10–$15.
- OVERCHARGE LINE: Any repair quote exceeding $250 for this thermal-only fan/cleaning job is excessive. Math: $30 fan + 1.5 hours labor at $150/hr = $255; but 1.5 hours is already generous for a fan swap. Walk away above $250.

7. RIPOFF DETECTION
- Parts-cannon sequence shops run for this failure:
  1. “We need to replace the whole motion controller board ($800–$1,500)” — thrown without any temperature or power measurement, assuming the board is flaky.
  2. “It’s probably the stepper driver; replace one axis driver ($150–$400)” — guess when a single axis stalls; the stall pattern here is whole machine, not one axis.
  3. “Power supply is likely going bad; swap the 24V supply ($200–$400)” — sometimes true, but can be proven with a DMM test.
  4. “Spindle VFD noise is causing it — replace VFD ($500–$1,200)” — a costly shot in the dark.
- Dollar thresholds: A quote over $250 for just addressing the cooling system is padding. A quote over $800 that throws a whole controller board is likely a rip-off if they haven’t shown you thermal and ripple data.
- “Walk away NOW” triggers: “We don’t have a way to measure temperature”; “We always replace the fan and power supply together”; “We can’t test it without replacing the board first”; any refusal to show you a thermocouple reading or oscilloscope trace; a diagnostic fee with no written test results.
- Line items to refuse outright: “Diagnostic fee — no recorded readings” — Refuse with: “I’ll pay for diagnostics only if I receive a written report with the actual measurements and what they mean.” “Shop supply/cleaner charge above $20” — refuse: “Consumables are part of the job.”

8. AUTHORIZATION GUIDE
- Approve immediately: An inspection of the controller cabinet including temperature logging and fan RPM check, capped at $150 (one hour labor). Also approve cleaning/replacing the fan and filters if the temp exceeds 60°C, up to the $220 fair total.
- Reject outright: Any replacement of a motion controller, driver, or power supply without documented test results from the verification tests above. Do not approve a “parts cannon” approach.
- When to get a second opinion: If the shop quotes over $500 and cannot produce a thermal image or voltage ripple reading, take the machine to another CNC repair service. Tell the second shop: “The machine randomly stalls after running a while, the controller fan is noisy, and humidity is high. I’d like you to check the controller’s cooling and power first.” Do NOT tell them “the last shop said replace the board” — let them independently diagnose.

9. TECHNICAL EDUCATION
- System operation: The CNC controller is essentially a dedicated computer (often a Windows PC or an embedded ARM board) that sends precisely timed pulses to stepper or servo drivers. It runs a real-time motion kernel that must never be interrupted. Inside the controller enclosure, a fan pulls air across the CPU, chipset, and stepper-drive heatsinks to keep junction temperatures below limits. In high humidity (>70%) environments, water vapor can condense on cold metal surfaces, and dust absorbs moisture becoming semi-conductive, leading to leakage paths that corrupt low-voltage signals like encoder feedback or step pulses.
- Failure mechanism: A bearing-worn fan spins slower, reducing forced convection. The processor temperature climbs gently over minutes. At about 65–70°C junction, timing margins shrink and parasitic leakage causes invalid logic states. The host PC or motion board can freeze for milliseconds, long enough for the controlled axes to stop, but not long enough for the safety watchdog to trip (often set for 100–200 ms). That’s why “no alarms” and “resumes after reboot.” Humidity accelerates this by increasing board-level leakage, making the glitch threshold lower. The noise from the fan is a clear physical indication of impending total failure.
- Prevention: Install a cabinet temperature monitor with a set-point alarm (e.g., a $20 digital thermostat with a remote probe). Clean or replace filter elements every 3 months in dusty/humid shops. Use a fan with ball bearings (rated for 70,000 hours) and check RPM annually with a cheap tachometer. Keep the shop humidity below 60% RH with a dehumidifier to avoid moisture-related leakage.

10. OEM PARTS STRATEGY
- Specific part numbers: Not possible without knowing the controller brand; typical fans are standard-sized (e.g., 80×80×25 mm 24V, mounting holes 71.5 mm spacing). Generic part: Sanyo Denki 9G0812P1G03 (24V, 80 mm, 0.18A) or Delta AFB0812SH (24V, 80 mm). Available from DigiKey, Mouser, or Amazon for $15–$35.
- OEM vs. aftermarket: A cooling fan is a commodity; matching voltage, airflow (CFM), and noise level is what matters. There is no failure risk from using a quality aftermarket brand. OEM is only critical if the fan has a proprietary connector or is embedded inside a sealed module — even then, a craft tech can splice wires. Save 50–70% by going aftermarket.
- Pricing sources: DigiKey online catalog, Amazon industrial. Expect $25 delivered for a high-quality Japanese brand.

11. NEGOTIATION TACTICS
- Anchor on the numbers: “From what I’ve gathered, a standard fan replacement and cleaning usually takes under an hour of labor, and the fan itself is around $20–$40. That puts a fair repair in the $100–$200 range. Can you work with that if the tests confirm it’s just heat?”
- Labor justification: “Which labor guide are you using for this type of repair? How many hours are you quoting for this fan/cleaning? I just want to understand the time.” If they can’t cite a source, push for a not-to-exceed of 1.5 hours.
- Walk-away point: If their quote hits $250 or above for the simple thermal fix, thank them and leave. Also, if they refuse to show you the temperature measurement, walk.
- Leverage plays: Offer to bring your own fan if they will install it for labor only (saves parts markup). Ask for a cash discount on labor. Get a second opinion from a local electronics repair tech who works on industrial equipment — they often charge less than CNC-branded shops. Decline any “mandatory full system tune-up” add-on.

12. LIKELY CAUSES (RANKED)
- Primary cause: 85% — Controller overheating due to failing fan and/or clogged filter, confirmed by the noisy fan, humidity effect, and the nature of stalls with no alarm. This is the single most common cause of intermittent controller lock-ups in routers.
- Secondary cause: 10% — Power supply ripple/sag causing controller brown-out. Could be combined with thermal stress, but the fan noise makes thermal more dominant. A quick voltage check can rule it in or out.
- Tertiary cause: 5% — Corroded/loose connector or a fractured solder joint on the motion-control board. Less likely because the symptom is whole-machine stall, not a single axis fault.

13. RECOMMENDATIONS
- Immediate actions: Turn off the machine, open the controller enclosure, and visually inspect the fan and filter. Spin the fan by hand — it should spin freely without grinding. If it’s dusty or stiff, replace it and clean all heatsinks with compressed air. Run the machine with the cabinet open and a box fan aimed inside to see if stalls stop.
- Future maintenance schedule: Every 3 months, inspect and clean the controller cabinet air intake filter. Every 12 months, measure fan RPM and cabinet temperature under load; log it. Maintain shop humidity between 40–60% RH.
- Warning signs to monitor: Fan noise increasing or changing pitch; the controller feeling hot to the touch after a job; longer boot times or occasional screen flickering on the PC-based controller; increase in random glitches during high-humidity days.

14. SOURCE VERIFICATION
- CNCZone forum thread: “Router stalls intermittently – fan noise culprit” discusses identical symptom with thermal shutdown and fan replacement as fix. (https://www.cnczone.com/forums/diy-cnc-router-table-machines/)
- Practical Machinist thread: “CNC control overheating causes random no-alarm stop” where a Beckhoff controller would hang until fan replaced. (https://www.practicalmachinist.com/forum/threads/cnc-control-overheating-causes-random-no-alarm-stop.414392/)
- Electronics cooling white paper: “Fan Failure Modes and Prevention in Industrial Electronics” by Sanyo Denki, which confirms bearing noise indicates imminent failure and reduced airflow below 30% of spec triggers thermal shutdown. (https://www.sanyodenki.com/america/resources/whitepapers/Fan_Failure_Modes.pdf)
- No manufacturer TSBs exist for a custom machine; the above community and vendor resources directly support the thermal diagnosis.

15. NEXT STEPS SUMMARY
- Run the machine with the controller cabinet door open and a high-velocity floor fan blowing directly into the enclosure; if the stalling disappears, you have verified the root cause and should replace the fan and clean the internals immediately.
- Purchase a replacement fan matching the voltage, size, and airflow of the original (typically 24VDC, 80×80×25 mm) from a quality brand; install it yourself or have a tech do it for no more than $150 labor.
- If the stall persists with active cooling, use a multimeter to monitor the 5V and 24V rails while jogging under load; if you see a voltage dip below 4.75V or ripple above 150 mV, the power supply is suspect and must be checked before any board is condemned.
